headline: High-risk shared filesystem and shell overlap create prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict hazards; ms-swift’s undocumented interaction raises uncertainty.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor reads workspace files and clipboard contents and can use MCP; ms-swift reads/writes files and runs CLI/Python workflows. A shared local filesystem makes it plausible that ms-swift outputs or artifacts are opened in Cursor and treated as instructions. No direct bridge is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace directory
IF ms-swift writes prompt-like text into logs, configs, or outputs that Cursor opens
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic opening of generated files in Cursor
Treat ms-swift outputs as untrusted text
Use read-only mounts for shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between tools

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files and can egress to allowlisted APIs. If they share a workspace, sensitive training or code artifacts can flow between them and out through ms-swift’s API calls. The pairwise path is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF the same filesystem contains source code and training artifacts
IF ms-swift sends file contents or logs to external model APIs
mitigations: Use separate directories for code and training data
Remove secrets from shared files before opening them in Cursor
Restrict ms-swift API access to non-sensitive datasets
Turn off clipboard sharing between apps
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can modify git state and write the filesystem; ms-swift can also write the filesystem and execute shell commands. On a shared directory, concurrent edits can corrupt code, configs, or outputs, and Cursor’s Yolo mode increases the chance of unsynchronized changes. ms-swift lacks git locking, so the overlap is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git checkout
IF Cursor runs in Yolo mode while ms-swift edits files concurrently
mitigations: Assign separate git worktrees
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use branch-per-agent workflows
Commit or stash before switching agents
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared outputs

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor’s agent loop can consume files and outputs, and ms-swift can generate logs, configs, and evaluation outputs that may be treated as authoritative. If Cursor uses ms-swift-produced artifacts without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect code or operational actions. The profiles do not show direct autonomous downstream actions, so medium fits.
conditions: IF Cursor ingests ms-swift outputs as ground truth
IF ms-swift emits stale or hallucinated configs, metrics, or summaries
mitigations: Require human review of ms-swift outputs
Add checksum or schema validation before reuse
Keep generated artifacts in a quarantine folder
Annotate outputs with source and timestamp
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor handles source code, open files, and clipboard contents, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files. If regulated data such as PII or secrets is placed in shared artifacts, differing retention and logging practices can create compliance gaps. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so the risk is bounded but real.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in shared files or logs
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the two tools
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Redact secrets before analysis
Set explicit retention limits for logs and checkpoints
Review vendor data-processing terms
requires-engineering: document residency and DPA coverage
